Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease of apple that spreads in cool, wet spring weather. The fungus survives winter in fallen infected leaves.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves, often along the veins
Spots darken; badly infected leaves turn yellow and drop early
Dark, rough, scabby spots on fruit, which may crack
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties
Rake up and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Prune to open the tree so leaves dry quickly after rain
treatment: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves and fruit
Protection is applied before infection, in spring — plan next season's program early

Apple___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that causes leaf spots, fruit rot and branch cankers. It survives in dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that grow into brown spots with purple edges ("frog-eye" leaf spot)
Fruit rot starting at the blossom end, turning brown to black; fruit shrivels into a mummy
Sunken, rough cankers on branches
prevention: Prune out dead wood and cankered branches
Remove mummified fruit from the tree and the ground
Keep trees vigorous and avoid wounding bark
treatment: Cut out infected branches well below the canker in dry weather and destroy them
Remove and destroy rotting and mummified fruit

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A rust fungus that needs both apple and juniper (eastern red cedar) trees to complete its life cycle. Spores blow from orange galls on junipers to apple leaves in spring.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper side of leaves in spring and early summer
Spots may get a red border; small tube-like growths form on the underside
Fruit can show similar spots and become deformed
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Where practical, remove nearby junipers or the galls on them
Check junipers in spring for orange, jelly-like galls
treatment: Infected leaves cannot be cured; protect new growth next spring
Remove galls from nearby junipers before they release spores

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.description: A fungal disease that grows on the surface of young leaves and fruit. It is favored by warm days, cool nights and high humidity, and does not need rain to spread.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves, often starting on young leaves
Leaves may curl, pucker or become distorted
A white powdery coating can also appear on fruit
prevention: Prune to improve air flow and sunlight in the canopy
Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer
Remove root suckers and water sprouts
treatment: Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots
Water at the base of the tree instead of over the leaves

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.description: A fungal leaf disease favored by warm, humid weather and corn residue left on the soil surface. It can reduce yield when upper leaves are affected.
symptoms: Small tan spots that grow into long, narrow, rectangular gray-to-tan lesions
Lesions run parallel to the leaf veins and stop at them
Severe cases kill whole leaves, starting from the lower leaves
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Rotate away from corn for at least one season
Manage crop residue where it is appropriate for your farm
treatment: Scout lower and middle leaves regularly before and after tasseling
Whether a spray is worthwhile depends on hybrid, weather and disease level — ask your extension officer

Corn___Common_rust.description: A rust fungus whose spores travel long distances on the wind. It is favored by cool, moist weather.
symptoms: Small, oval or elongated cinnamon-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf
Pustules break open and release powdery, rust-colored spores
Pustules turn dark brown to black late in the season
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Follow local advice on planting dates
treatment: Field corn with good resistance usually needs no treatment
Sweet corn and susceptible varieties may need protection — ask your extension officer

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A fungal leaf disease favored by moderate temperatures and long periods of leaf wetness. It survives in infected corn residue.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions, about 2.5–15 cm long
Lesions appear first on lower leaves and move upward
Dark spores may form on lesions in humid weather
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Rotate crops
Manage infected crop residue
treatment: Scout fields regularly, especially around tasseling
Ask your extension officer whether control is worthwhile for your field

Grape___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that can destroy grape clusters in warm, wet weather. It survives winter in mummified berries and infected canes.
symptoms: Reddish-brown round spots on leaves with dark borders and tiny black dots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard, black "mummies"
Long black lesions on shoots and leaf stalks
prevention: Remove mummified berries from vines and the ground
Prune and train vines for good air flow and sunlight
Keep weeds under control around vines
treatment: Remove and destroy infected clusters, leaves and canes

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Complex of wood-infecting fungi, including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A trunk disease of grapevines. Fungi infect the wood through pruning wounds and slowly damage the vine over years.
symptoms: "Tiger-stripe" leaves: yellow or red areas between the veins that dry and turn brown
Small dark spots on berries ("measles")
Sudden wilting and drying of the whole vine in hot weather
Dark streaks in the wood when the trunk is cut
prevention: Prune in dry weather and protect large pruning wounds
Remove and destroy dead vines and infected wood
Plant healthy, certified planting material
treatment: There is no cure for infected vines
Cutting back to healthy wood or retraining a new trunk can help some vines

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A fungal leaf spot disease favored by warm, humid conditions. Severe infection can cause early leaf drop.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown to black spots on leaves
Spots may have a yellow edge and join into large dead areas
Early leaf drop in severe cases
prevention: Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves
Prune and train vines to improve air flow
Avoid overhead irrigation
treatment: Remove severely infected leaves

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: "Candidatus Liberibacter" bacteria, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A serious, incurable bacterial disease of citrus, spread by a small insect (the Asian citrus psyllid) and by infected plant material.
symptoms: Blotchy, uneven yellow mottling on leaves, different on each side of the midrib
Yellow shoots and twig dieback
Small, lopsided, poorly colored, bitter fruit that may drop early
prevention: Buy only certified disease-free nursery trees
Monitor for and control the Asian citrus psyllid
Do not move citrus plants or cuttings out of affected areas
treatment: There is no cure; infected trees decline and are usually removed
In many countries this disease must be reported — contact your local plant protection office

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease spread by wind-driven rain. It damages leaves, twigs and fruit, especially on susceptible varieties.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown
Spot centers fall out ("shot holes"); leaves may yellow and drop
Sunken dark spots and cracks on fruit
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Keep trees healthy, but avoid too much nitrogen
Use windbreaks where wind-driven rain is common
treatment: Prune out infected twigs during dry weather
Ask your extension officer about protective sprays for your area

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease carried on seed and plant debris and spread by splashing water. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown, often with a yellow halo
Leaves may yellow and drop
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2–3 years
Avoid overhead watering and do not work with plants when they are wet
treatment: Remove and destroy badly infected plants and debris
Clean and disinfect tools and stakes

Potato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease that usually starts on older leaves, especially on stressed plants. It survives in plant debris and soil.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with rings inside (like a target) on older, lower leaves
Yellowing around the spots; affected leaves may die
Dark, sunken, dry spots on tubers
prevention: Rotate crops: avoid potato and tomato on the same land for 2–3 years
Use healthy seed tubers; keep plants well fed and watered
Remove plant debris after harvest
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves
Ask your extension officer whether protective sprays are needed

Potato___Late_blight.description: A very destructive disease that spreads quickly in cool, wet weather and can kill a field in days. Spores travel long distances on the wind.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked patches on leaves that quickly turn brown or black
White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid weather
Firm, reddish-brown rot in tubers
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles
Hill soil well over tubers; grow resistant varieties
treatment: Act fast: remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost them)
Warn neighboring growers — the disease spreads on the wind
Harvest only after vines are fully dead, to protect tubers

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A very common fungal disease of squash and other cucurbits. It spreads on the wind and does not need wet leaves to infect.
symptoms: White, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves
Spots spread until whole leaves are covered
Leaves yellow, brown and die early; fruit may get sunburned
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Space plants for good air flow and grow them in full sun
Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer
treatment: Remove badly infected leaves

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A fungal leaf disease that survives on infected leaves and spreads by splashing water.
symptoms: Many small, irregular purple to dark red spots on the upper leaf surface
Spots join and leaves look burned (scorched), curl and dry
Spot centers stay dark (they do not turn white)
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and certified healthy plants
Renovate beds after harvest and remove old leaves
Use drip irrigation instead of wetting the leaves
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease carried on seed and plant debris and spread by splashing water. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, sometimes with a yellow halo
Leaves may yellow and drop
Small, raised, scabby spots on fruit
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2–3 years
Avoid overhead watering and do not work with plants when they are wet
treatment: Remove and destroy badly infected plants and debris
Clean and disinfect tools and stakes

Tomato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease that starts on older leaves and moves up the plant. It survives in plant debris and soil.
symptoms: Brown spots with rings inside (like a target) on older, lower leaves
Yellowing around the spots; leaves may drop
Dark, sunken spots on stems and near the stem end of fruit
prevention: Rotate crops: avoid tomato and potato on the same land for 2–3 years
Mulch the soil and stake plants so leaves don't touch the ground
Remove plant debris after harvest
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves
Ask your extension officer whether protective sprays are needed

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A very destructive disease that spreads quickly in cool, wet weather. The same organism attacks potato.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy gray-green patches on leaves that turn brown
White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid weather
Brown patches on stems; firm, greasy brown areas on fruit
prevention: Use healthy transplants; keep tomatoes away from potatoes
Avoid overhead watering
Grow resistant varieties where available
treatment: Act fast: remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost them)
Warn neighboring growers — the disease spreads on the wind

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease mostly found in greenhouses and tunnels, favored by high humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper side of leaves
Olive-green to gray velvety mold on the underside, below the spots
Leaves turn yellow, wither and drop
prevention: Lower humidity: ventilate greenhouses and tunnels
Space and prune plants for air flow
Grow resistant varieties
treatment: Remove infected leaves
Clean greenhouse structures between crops

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A common fungal leaf disease spread by splashing water. It survives on plant debris and weeds.
symptoms: Many small round spots with dark borders and gray or tan centers
Tiny black dots inside the spots
Starts on lower leaves; heavy infection makes leaves yellow and drop
prevention: Rotate crops and remove plant debris
Mulch the soil to stop splashing
Water at the base of plants, not over the leaves
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves
Ask your extension officer whether protective sprays are needed

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.pathogen: Tetranychus urticae (a mite pest, not a disease)
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves. They multiply very fast in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white speckles on leaves
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves and on stems
Leaves turn bronze, dry out and fall in heavy infestations
prevention: Check leaf undersides often, especially in hot, dry weather
Keep plants well watered and reduce dust
Protect natural enemies such as predatory mites by avoiding unnecessary sprays
treatment: Spray leaf undersides with a strong jet of water to knock mites off
Remove heavily infested leaves

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease of warm, humid regions that affects leaves, stems and fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with lighter centers and rings inside on leaves
Spots join, leaves yellow and drop
Sunken brown spots on fruit that may crack
prevention: Rotate crops and remove plant debris
Prune and space plants for air flow
Avoid overhead watering
treatment: Remove infected leaves

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A very stable virus that spreads by touch — on hands, tools and clothing — and can be carried on seed.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves
Leaves may be curled, distorted or fern-like
Stunted plants and uneven fruit ripening
prevention: Grow resistant varieties and use clean seed
Wash hands and disinfect tools when working with plants
Do not use tobacco while handling plants
treatment: There is no cure for virus-infected plants
Remove and destroy infected plants; do not compost them

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), spread by whiteflies
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A virus spread by the silverleaf whitefly. Plants infected young may produce almost no fruit.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward, stay small and have yellow edges
Plants are stunted and bushy
Flowers drop and very little fruit forms
prevention: Grow resistant varieties
Use whitefly-free transplants; protect seedlings with insect-proof netting
Control weeds that host whiteflies
treatment: There is no cure for virus-infected plants
Remove and destroy infected plants early to slow spread
